questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the real difference between "deploy" and "release"?
options: They are two different names for exactly the same event, with no practical distinction
Deploy only applies to databases; release only applies to application code
Deploy means new code is now running in production infrastructure; release means users can actually see and use the new behavior — a separate decision
Release always happens before deploy, never after it
questions.explain: In a naive pipeline these happen at the same moment, but feature flags exist specifically to break that coupling — code can be fully deployed while the behavior it enables stays off for every user.

questions.q: What is a feature flag, in the terms this lesson uses?
options: A runtime check, usually backed by a flag-management service, that decides per request or per user whether a given code path executes
A comment in the source code that documents what a function does
A Kubernetes label applied only during the build stage
A type of integration test that runs before the scan stage
questions.explain: The flag check happens at request time — flagClient.getContext(...) plus isEnabled(...) in the example — deciding live whether the new or legacy code path runs, independent of what's deployed.

questions.q: What does this lesson say a feature flag's "kill switch" capability provides that a rollback of deployed infrastructure does not?
options: It permanently deletes the feature's code from the repository
It requires a full new pipeline run through build, test, and scan before it takes effect
It only works for features that have never been deployed yet
Flipping the flag off is immediate, with no redeploy and no waiting for a pipeline to run — the code stays deployed, it's just no longer active for users
questions.explain: Because the flag check happens at runtime, turning a feature off is just flipping a value the flag-management service serves — no CI pipeline, no infrastructure rollback, and no wait for a deploy to propagate.

questions.q: In the flag targeting rule example — `{"if": "user.segment == 'internal'", "serve": true}` plus a 5% rollout bucket rule — what is actually being controlled?
options: Which Kubernetes namespace the pods are scheduled into
Which users see the new behavior, based on who they are — independent of which servers or pods are running the code
Which container registry the image is pulled from
How many CPU cores the deployment is allowed to use
questions.explain: This operates at the application layer, targeting by user identity or segment, which is a different axis entirely from canary's infrastructure-layer traffic percentage — the two can run independently of each other.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a team with canary deployments and automated rollback still benefits from feature flags?
options: Canary and automated rollback operate on deployed code and infrastructure traffic, but can't control which specific users see a fully released feature, or instantly disable it without touching infrastructure at all
Feature flags are only useful for teams that have no CI/CD pipeline at all
Canary deployments and feature flags are mutually exclusive and cannot be used on the same service
Automated rollback already makes feature flags completely unnecessary in every case
questions.explain: A canary rollout can shift infrastructure traffic to a new version while a risky feature inside it stays behind a flag released to only a small percentage of users — the two mechanisms work at different layers and complement each other.
